classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly requested diagonal method by flipping each diagonal bit and explain why the resulting sequence escapes every listed entry.

content.prompt: Consider the set of all infinite sequences of zeroes and ones. Using Cantor’s diagonalisation argument, show that this set is not countable.

answer.short:
The set is uncountable.

For any proposed list, change each diagonal entry to construct a binary sequence differing from every listed sequence.
answer.worked:
Suppose the set is countable, so all its sequences can be listed as
$$\begin{align*}s_1&=(a_{11},a_{12},a_{13},\ldots),\\s_2&=(a_{21},a_{22},a_{23},\ldots),\\s_3&=(a_{31},a_{32},a_{33},\ldots),\\&\vdots\end{align*}$$
where every $a_{ij}$ is either $0$ or $1$.

Construct the binary sequence $s=(b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots)$ by setting $b_n=1-a_{nn}$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus, replace each diagonal $0$ by $1$ and each diagonal $1$ by $0$.

For every $n$, the sequence $s$ differs from $s_n$ at its $n$th entry. Therefore, $s$ is an infinite binary sequence absent from the purported complete list. This contradiction proves that the set is uncountable.
